---
title: "The Short Story"
subtitle: "How a system like ChatGPT is built, what exists once training is finished, and what happens to your text when you type, in about twenty minutes"
---

## The question

If you type something into a system like ChatGPT, what exists on the
other side, how was it created, and what actually happens to your text?

A [language model](glossary.qmd#language-model) is a large mathematical
function controlled by a very large collection of learned
[parameters](glossary.qmd#parameter); modern large models contain
billions of them. Creating one starts with assembling and preparing
text, then using that text to train a neural network to predict
[tokens](glossary.qmd#token), the small units the text is cut into.
[S-05] [Post-training](glossary.qmd#post-training) then changes those
same parameters so that the model becomes far more useful for following
instructions. [S-55] When you later type into a ChatGPT-like product,
the parameters normally stay fixed. Your message becomes part of the
model's [context](glossary.qmd#context), the model generates tokens one
at a time, and software around the model can add retrieval, tools,
external state, and repeated calls. [S-31] [S-56]

{{< include _includes/_fig-lifecycle.qmd >}}

Pretraining and post-training are both training, because both update
the model's parameters. Everything after the post-trained model leaves
the parameters alone: it changes what the model is given and what is
done with its output.

## 1. What the finished object is

Stripped of the surrounding product, a runnable open language model is
two things: code that implements the neural-network computation, and a
checkpoint file holding the learned parameters. Andrej Karpathy's 2023
general-audience introduction opens with this picture, using an open
model as the example: a large file of parameters, and a small program
that runs the network with them. [S-75] His `llama2.c` repository shows
the same division literally, as a single C inference file for the Llama
2 architecture that needs a model checkpoint before it can generate
anything. [S-82] The file count varies by product and deployment; the
division of labor does not. The code specifies how the computation
works. Training discovers the parameter values. The information the
model learned during training is distributed across those values.

{{< include _includes/_fig-runnable-model.qmd >}}

Using the model is called [inference](glossary.qmd#inference): the code
runs with the parameter values fixed and computes a probability
distribution over the next token. Ordinary inference does not change
the parameters, so the rest of this page divides into how the
parameters get their values, and what the surrounding software does
with the finished object.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §8 on what does and
does not change the parameters.
:::

## 2. The smallest piece of a neural network

The smallest useful piece of a neural network is one learned
transformation:

$$
h = \sigma(Wx + b)
$$

$x$ is a list of incoming numbers. $W$ and $b$ are learned parameters:
$W$ multiplies the inputs, forming a weighted sum, and $b$ shifts the
result. $\sigma$ is a fixed nonlinear function applied to that sum. $h$
is the newly computed representation, another list of numbers, ready to
be the $x$ of the next step. [S-12] This is not "the equation for
ChatGPT". It is the basic pattern from which much larger networks are
built.

{{< include _includes/_fig-tiny-network.qmd >}}

Larger [neural networks](glossary.qmd#neural-network) combine many such
learned transformations and nonlinear operations, arranged in layers,
with millions or billions of parameters chosen by training rather than
by a person. This one-line example is the smallest case to keep in
mind. A language model is a particular, enormous network of this kind,
and the object it computes can be written as

$$
p_\theta(\text{next token} \mid \text{context})
$$

where $\theta$ stands for the entire collection of learned parameters,
the [transformer](glossary.qmd#transformer) architecture (§5) defines
the huge function that uses them, and the output is a probability
distribution over every possible next token given the text so far.
Whenever "parameters", "training", or "the network" appears below, it
refers to $\theta$, to the process that sets $\theta$, or to the function
that uses $\theta$.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
works one unit through by hand, including one full training step.
:::

## 3. Assembling the text the model learns from

The first step in creating a language model is assembling the text it
will learn from. That text does not arrive ready to use. Source material
is gathered from web pages, code, books, and other permitted sources;
the main text is extracted from its raw form, stripped of navigation
menus and markup; documents are filtered by language and by quality
rules; duplicates are removed, because the same page copied a thousand
times would otherwise be learned a thousand times; and only the
surviving text is handed to the tokenizer. What ends up in that corpus
shapes what the model can learn, and every step involves choices.

{{< include _includes/_fig-data-pipeline.qmd >}}

Hugging Face's FineWeb dataset is one open example of such a pipeline.
It is built from Common Crawl web snapshots by filtering URLs,
extracting the main text of each page, keeping English text, applying
quality filters, and removing duplicates, and the whole recipe is
published. [S-78] It is one example, not a template. Complete training
corpora for closed models are often not publicly disclosed, the level of
disclosure varies across models and providers, corpora differ between
models, and no model trains on "the whole internet". This is why the
shorthand "trained on the internet" hides a substantial data-engineering
pipeline.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §1 on the
corpus, then §3 onward for what happens to it. For the full engineering
lifecycle, including data pipelines, see Stanford CS336 in
[resources](resources.qmd).
:::

## 4. From text to tokens to vectors

A neural network computes with numbers, so the corpus, and later your
message, has to be converted. The [tokenizer](glossary.qmd#tokenizer)
cuts text into tokens drawn from a fixed
[vocabulary](glossary.qmd#vocabulary) decided before training. A token
may be a whole word, a fragment of one, punctuation, or another piece
the tokenizer defines; in many commonly used subword tokenizers a
preceding space affects the token. [S-28] Each token is then replaced by
its index in the vocabulary, its [token ID](glossary.qmd#token-id). With
made-up numbers, "cat" might become 812 and "dog" 913.

Those two integers are arbitrary addresses. They do not mean that dog is
larger than cat, or 101 units away from it, or that tokens with nearby
IDs have related meanings; a different tokenizer would assign entirely
different numbers to the same pieces. So the network should not treat
the ID itself as a meaningful quantity, and it does not. The ID selects
one row of a learned matrix, the [embedding](glossary.qmd#embedding)
table $E$, and that row, $E[812]$ for "cat", is a vector of learned
numbers. The entries of $E$ are parameters. Training changes them
because changing them can improve next-token prediction, and by the end
of training tokens that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar
rows. [S-29] [S-30] That is what the lookup buys: instead of an address,
the network receives numbers it can transform and combine.

{{< include _includes/_fig-token-to-vector.qmd >}}

The row is only the starting point. The embedding for `␣bank` (the
leading space is part of the token) is the same wherever the token
occurs, but the transformer's layers then update
each position using the positions around it, so that in "the river bank"
and "the central bank" the same starting vector ends as two different
[contextual representations](glossary.qmd#contextual-representation).
Section 5 explains the mechanism that does this. Mathematically, an
embedding lookup is the same as multiplying a vector that is all zeros
except for a single one at the token's position by the matrix $E$; in
practice, the implementation simply retrieves the row. [S-86] The
tokenizer is not the model and is not trained by the same process: its
splitting rules are fixed before training, while $E$ is part of $\theta$
and is learned.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) traces one
sentence through these steps;
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
explains why the vocabulary is made of fragments.
:::

## 5. From recurrent networks to the transformer

Neural networks were already being used to predict language before
transformers. An influential 2003 model learned a vector for each word
together with a network that predicted the next word, trained by the
same kind of objective the transformer uses today. [S-29] [S-41] For
sequences, [recurrent networks](glossary.qmd#recurrent-network),
including LSTMs, became established and highly influential approaches.
[S-21] A recurrent network passes a running state from one position to
the next. To relate two distant positions, information has to travel
through every intervening step, and each step's computation depends on
the previous one having finished. During training that dependency limits
how much can be computed in parallel, and it makes the path between
distant positions long. [S-16]

{{< include _includes/_fig-rnn-vs-transformer.qmd >}}

Attention gives a position a direct way to combine information from the
other positions it is permitted to use. It works in short steps. The
model transforms the destination's representation into a query vector.
It transforms each permitted source's representation into a key vector.
Comparing the query with each key produces a score. Softmax converts
those scores into nonnegative weights that sum to one. Each source also
provides a value vector, a transformed representation carrying the
information to be combined. The weighted combination of those values
supplies the information used to update the destination's
representation. [S-36] In "The animal crossed the street because it was
tired", the representation at "it" can draw heavily on "animal" and
lightly on the rest, in a single step, without relaying anything
through the positions in between.

{{< include _includes/_fig-attention-intuition.qmd >}}

The three transformations, into queries, keys, and values, are learned
matrices: parameters set by training. The attention weights are not
parameters; they are computed afresh for each input from those
transformed vectors. [S-36] An attention weight is a local mixing weight
inside one head at one layer, not a causal explanation of the model's
output, and real models run many heads in parallel and stack many
layers, so no single weight tells you why the model said what it said.
[S-37] [S-45]

Attention came before the transformer. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio used a
learned weighted selection over source positions in a neural
translation system, in work posted in 2014 and presented at ICLR 2015.
[S-68] Vaswani and colleagues' 2017 paper, *Attention Is All You Need*,
then built a sequence architecture around attention and per-position
feed-forward computation, without recurrence, at a time when recurrent
networks were the established state of the art. [S-21] [S-23] In one
layer any position can read any permitted earlier position directly,
and during training on a known sequence the positions within a layer
can be computed in parallel; generation itself still proceeds one token
at a time. [S-17]

A transformer is not attention alone, and it is not the beginning of
neural networks. Each repeating block contains two kinds of computation:
[self-attention](glossary.qmd#self-attention), which moves information
between positions, and a feed-forward layer, which computes on each
position separately using the pattern from §2. A model stacks many such
blocks. [S-19] In the causal decoder models this course is about, a
position may attend to itself and earlier positions, never later ones.
[S-22]

Removing much of the recurrent sequential dependency made training substantially
more parallelizable, and the paper notes that its attention can be
implemented with highly optimized matrix-multiplication code, the kind
of computation that GPUs and later accelerators perform well. [S-23]
That fit was one reason among several that transformers became
dominant, alongside scale, training data, and the surrounding software
ecosystem; this course does not attempt a hardware history. [S-20] Dense
attention also has its own cost, growing with the square of the
sequence length. [S-17]

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) for the
argument and the paper's own figures;
[How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
for the arithmetic on a three-token example;
[Milestones](milestones.qmd) for the history.
:::

## 6. Pretraining makes the base model

Pretraining is the first and largest parameter-learning phase. The
corpus is tokenized, and at every position the model is asked to predict
the next token; the text itself supplies the answer, so no one has to
label anything. A [loss](glossary.qmd#loss) measures how little
probability the model gave to the token that actually came next.
[Backpropagation](glossary.qmd#backpropagation) computes the gradient of
the loss with respect to the trainable parameters, that is, how the loss
would change with a small change in them. An
[optimizer](glossary.qmd#optimizer) uses those gradients to nudge
$\theta$. Then the next batch of text, and the next, on a scale hard to
picture. [S-05] [S-14] [S-40]

```
token sequences → next-token predictions → loss
      → backpropagation computes gradients → optimizer updates θ → repeat
```

The architecture and the optimization procedure are specified in code;
training is the process that discovers the parameter values. The result
is the [base model](glossary.qmd#base-model). Because predicting text
well requires capturing its regularities, the base model has broad
statistical knowledge of grammar, meaning, recurring facts, and
conventions of argument, and language models trained only to predict
text have been observed to perform tasks such as answering questions
and translating without being trained for them. [S-44] [S-26] A base
model is not a database that reliably retrieves records from its
training corpus. It can nevertheless memorize and sometimes reproduce
passages from that data: researchers have extracted verbatim training
text from a public model, including sequences that appeared in only one
training document. [S-87] Generation is not reliable lookup, and nothing
in the objective checks truth. [S-08] The base model is also not
specifically optimized to behave as a conversational assistant. Given an
instruction, it may answer it, continue it, or produce more instructions
like it, because all of those follow such text somewhere in the corpus.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) sets out the
objective, the loss, the loop, and what they do and do not teach.
:::

## 7. Post-training shapes assistant behavior

Post-training changes the same parameter collection $\theta$, with the
same machinery of loss, gradients, and optimizer. No new kind of network
appears. What changes is the data and the objective. [S-55]

The simplest form, [supervised fine-tuning](glossary.qmd#supervised-fine-tuning),
trains on curated conversations: a prompt, and the response the builders
want. The loss is the same next-token loss as pretraining, applied to
the response tokens, so that after training a request is far more
likely to be treated as a request. Preference-based stages go further:
candidate responses are compared, and the parameters are updated toward
the preferred behavior, either through a learned
[reward model](glossary.qmd#reward-model) and
[reinforcement learning](glossary.qmd#reinforcement-learning) (the route
usually called [RLHF](glossary.qmd#rlhf)) or directly from the comparison
pairs. [S-46] [S-47] The influential 2022 recipe used human-written
demonstrations and human comparisons; published modern recipes can also
use synthetic or model-generated data and feedback produced by models,
rules, or automatic checks, as Constitutional AI and the DeepSeek-R1
report each illustrate, so "post-training data" does not simply mean
"text written by human labelers". [S-48] [S-49] The methods vary between
providers and change over time, and they share one thing: they update
parameters.

{{< include _includes/_fig-training-stages.qmd >}}

::: {.analogy-callout}
Useful analogy, not the mechanism

Karpathy's 2025 deep dive organizes the training stages with a classroom
picture: pretraining is like reading expository text to acquire
background knowledge; supervised fine-tuning is like studying worked
examples; reinforcement learning on checkable tasks is like solving
practice problems against an answer key. [S-76] The analogy is useful for
two reasons. It explains why later stages use more targeted data and
feedback than pretraining, and it separates imitating demonstrations
from trial and error against a checkable outcome. Human learning and
neural-network optimization are biologically and mechanistically
different; the analogy organizes the stages, and it is not a theory that
language models learn the way people do.
:::

The instructions a product places in front of your conversation, its
[system prompt](glossary.qmd#system-prompt), are not post-training. They
are text in the context, and they change nothing in the model. [S-31]

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) describes the family
of methods and keeps its members straight.
:::

## 8. Fluency, abstention, and evidence

A fluent assistant can state something false, and the reason is in the
training objective rather than in a defect that post-training added.
Pretraining rewards assigning probability to whatever came next in the
text and contains no independent check of truth, so false or unsupported
continuations are already possible before any post-training. [S-08]
Post-training then makes instruction-following and question-answering
behavior much more likely. A model can therefore produce a well-formed
answer even when the information encoded in its parameters is
insufficient, because nothing in the mechanism asks whether it is.
Depending on the recipe, post-training can also explicitly encourage
abstention, calibrated uncertainty, truthfulness, or tool use.
Post-training did not create the possibility of unsupported answers; it
changed the default form of the response.

Post-training can include examples in which the right response is to
say "I don't know" or to ask for more information, so that abstention
becomes a likely response when the model's own knowledge is thin.
Retrieval and tools can ground an answer in external, inspectable
evidence, a document or a search result placed in the context at
inference time, rather than relying only on information encoded
imperfectly in $\theta$. [S-33] That evidence still has to be evaluated:
retrieval can return irrelevant or incorrect material, and a tool result
verifies only what it was asked. Karpathy's introductions make the
first point in plain language, as a pedagogical intuition: fine-tuning
does not remove a model's tendency to produce confident inventions, it
"directs" that tendency toward helpful assistant behavior, and retrieved
material in the context window changes what the answer can rest on.
[S-75] [S-77] Fluency is not evidence, and evidence beats confidence.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §7 on prediction
versus verification; [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd)
§4–§6 on sources of truth and verification.
:::

## 9. What happens when you type

When you send a request, the trained model generates its response one
token at a time. With the post-trained model built and its parameters
fixed, here is one request followed all the way through.

1. You type text. The surrounding product assembles and manages the
   [context window](glossary.qmd#context-window) for this call: its
   system prompt, the conversation so far, any documents or tool results
   it has decided to include, and your new message. [S-31]
2. The tokenizer converts that text into token IDs. [S-28]
3. Each ID selects its embedding vector from the table $E$.
4. The vectors pass through the transformer blocks; at each block,
   attention lets every position use the permitted earlier positions,
   and the feed-forward layer computes on each position. [S-19]
5. After the last block, the vector at the final position is turned into
   one raw score per vocabulary entry (machine-learning literature calls
   these scores [logits](glossary.qmd#logit)). [S-05]
6. [Softmax](glossary.qmd#softmax) turns the scores into a probability
   distribution; a setting called [temperature](glossary.qmd#temperature)
   controls how concentrated it is.
7. A [decoding](glossary.qmd#decoding) rule selects the next token,
   deterministically or stochastically. [S-07]
8. That token is appended to the context, and the next step runs on the
   extended sequence.
9. Repeat until the model produces a stop token or a limit is reached.
   A paragraph of output is this loop, one token at a time.

{{< include _includes/_fig-inference-loop.qmd >}}

At every step the parameters do not change: ordinary inference never
updates $\theta$. The system prompt and any supplied documents are
context, not retraining. Implementations typically reuse cached
intermediate results for the earlier positions, the keys and values that
attention computed, rather than recomputing them at every step. [S-43]
When stochastic decoding ([sampling](glossary.qmd#sampling)) is used, it
is one reason repeated runs from the same context can produce different
continuations without anything in the model having changed.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](learn/softmax-sampling.qmd)
for the equation and an interactive; [How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd)
§9 on why training and generation are different computations.
:::

## 10. Reasoning-oriented models: training, and thinking longer at inference

A reasoning-oriented model can use additional generation steps before
producing its final answer. Some such models receive additional reinforcement learning
on problems whose outcomes can be checked automatically, such as
mathematics problems with known answers or code with tests. An
automatically checkable or rule-based outcome can supply a reward
without requiring a learned reward model for that reward component, and
reinforcement learning against such rewards can encourage useful
intermediate reasoning before the final answer. In the published
DeepSeek-R1 case, this was associated with better performance on
reasoning tasks and with steadily longer intermediate reasoning traces;
R1-Zero, which applied reinforcement learning directly to the pretrained
base model with no supervised fine-tuning step first, suffered from poor
readability and language mixing, and the released R1 model used a
multi-stage recipe that also included supervised stages. [S-49]
This is one post-training route used in some reasoning-oriented models,
not a stage every model goes through, and recipes differ between
providers.

Training is only half of what "a model that thinks longer" means. Once
training is finished, the parameters remain fixed. A reasoning-oriented
model can nevertheless spend more computation on a difficult request by
generating additional intermediate reasoning tokens before producing the
final answer. The next-token mechanism did not disappear: the
intermediate reasoning is generated sequentially by the same model, and
each intermediate token becomes part of the context that the following
computation conditions on. That gives the model more sequential
inference-time computation before it commits to an answer. It is not
another training round, and the parameters do not change. [S-83]

{{< include _includes/_fig-reasoning-compute.qmd >}}

Many modern reasoning-oriented models can spend additional
inference-time computation in this way before producing a final
response, and providers expose the choice in different ways, such as a
reasoning-effort setting or a thinking level. The documentation of
Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, read on 2026-09-15, each describes its
own models generating reasoning before the answer, a control for how
much, and reasoning tokens that are counted and billed like output.
[S-83] [S-84] [S-85] On some difficult tasks, generating intermediate
[reasoning tokens](glossary.qmd#reasoning-tokens) provides additional
inference-time computation and can improve performance. The tokens are
output, produced by the same next-token mechanism as any other output.
They are not a transcript of the model's internal computation. What a
product exposes of intermediate reasoning varies by model and interface,
and a displayed explanation should not be treated as a guaranteed
faithful record of the underlying computation; Anthropic's announcement
of its feature states that what appears in the thought process is not
guaranteed to represent what is going on inside the model. [S-49] [S-83]
[S-84] [S-85] And the tokens are not thought in the human sense.

Reasoning also connects to tools. A model can reason, generate a request
for a tool, have the surrounding software execute it, receive the
observation into its context, and continue reasoning with the new
evidence before answering or requesting another tool; Anthropic's and
OpenAI's current documentation both describe reasoning interleaved with
tool calls in this way. [S-83] [S-85] The reasoning never executes
anything itself; §12 walks through one such round trip.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §7.
:::

## 11. Parameters, context, and external state

The model can also use information supplied in the current context or
returned by tools. A model can carry useful information in three very
different places.
Training encodes statistical information in the parameters, which are
inside the model and change only when it is trained. A request puts
information directly into the current context: for each model step, the
surrounding system supplies or manages a finite inference-time context,
the sequence of tokens the model conditions on for that step. And
software can keep information outside the model, as
[external state](glossary.qmd#external-state) such as files, a database,
saved notes, or a stored summary of an earlier session, and supply it
again later. Information persisted across sessions is maintained outside
the model and may be retrieved or supplied again on later steps;
persistence alone does not update model parameters. [S-31]

{{< include _includes/_fig-three-stores.qmd >}}

All three are sometimes described informally as "memory", which is why
the word can be confusing; a product that "remembers" your project has
stored something outside the model and supplied it again, and no
parameter was updated. [Retrieval](glossary.qmd#retrieval) is the general
name for bringing external information into the context, from a
document collection, a search, a file, or a store. It changes this
call's inputs, never the parameters. [S-33]

::: {.analogy-callout}
Useful analogy, not the mechanism

Karpathy's introductions describe the context window as the model's
"working memory". [S-75] [S-77] Building on that framing, a useful course
analogy is to think of parametric knowledge as imperfect long-term recall
and explicit context as material currently in working memory, directly
in front of the system for this call. It is an intuition about why
supplying a document works better than hoping the model "knows" its
contents. Analogy, not mechanism: it is not a claim that the network has
memory systems like a person's.
:::

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§8–§10; [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7.
:::

## 12. Tools, and the loop that makes an agentic system

Suppose you ask an assistant, "What is the weather in Bogotá today?" The
model's parameters cannot contain today's weather, and a model call by
itself does not read a file, run a program, search the web, or send
anything. What makes an answer possible is that the software around the
model has described an available weather [tool](glossary.qmd#tool) in
the context, with its name, what it does, and the inputs it takes.
Instead of inventing a value, the model generates structured output that
means, roughly, `call weather(location="Bogotá")`. The surrounding
software recognizes that request, checks it against its permission
rules, and runs the weather tool. The tool returns a result; suppose,
for this example only, that it returns `18 °C, light rain`. The software
places that result into the context of a later model call, and the model
reads it and writes the answer. [S-51]

The model requested the action. Software executed it. The result became
new context. At the model boundary, a [tool call](glossary.qmd#tool-call)
is generated output in a structured format, and everything that happens
between the request and the result is performed outside the model.

{{< include _includes/_fig-tool-roundtrip.qmd >}}

Repeat that round trip under a controlling loop and you have the minimal
mechanism behind what this course calls an agentic system. An objective
and the current context go to the model; the model produces a tool
request or a response; a request is checked and executed; the
observation updates the context; the model is called again; and the
loop continues, asks you, or stops.

{{< include _includes/_fig-agent-loop.qmd >}}

Nothing new appears inside the model at this stage. The same network,
the same fixed parameters, and the same next-token prediction are
invoked repeatedly by software that carries the state between calls.
[S-56] The word [agent](glossary.qmd#agent) has no universally fixed
boundary; a system whose steps are mostly written in advance is better
called a [workflow](glossary.qmd#workflow), and the simplest system that
reliably solves the task is usually the right one. [S-50]

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) walks through one
tool call and one whole task, with state, skills, verification, and
permissions.
:::

## 13. The mental model

A language model is a learned next-token predictor: code plus a large
collection of parameters. A curated corpus was tokenized and used in
pretraining to set those parameters so that they capture the structure
of text; post-training changed them further, with the same machinery on
different data, so that the model behaves as an assistant. Once trained,
the parameters are fixed; the request-specific information the model
conditions on is supplied through inference-time context, and decoding
settings and surrounding product logic can also affect the output
without changing a parameter. Software around the model can give it
retrieval, tools, and persistent state, and can call it repeatedly, and
that loop of model step, action, and evidence is what turns a predictor
into a system that carries out work.

Four consequences follow for anyone who uses such a system. Fluency is
not evidence: the output is a plausible continuation, whether or not
anything was checked. Tool use is not automatically
[verification](glossary.qmd#verification): a tool was used only if a
request was executed, and it verified only what it was asked to verify.
A passing check proves only what that check tested. And models and tools
can assist judgment, by organizing evidence, testing alternatives, and
checking mechanical claims, but on judgment-heavy questions the system's
output does not itself establish that the conclusion is warranted;
evidence, review, and human accountability remain necessary.

::: {.go-deeper}
Go deeper: [Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) turns these
into working habits; the [glossary](glossary.qmd) defines every term used
above.
:::
